about: Bug or clean? Each ball carries a short function (or a circuit step) and what it should do. Dodge the bugs, catch the clean ones. Python items carry a `check` that tests/test_gym_games.py runs: it passes for clean items and fails for buggy ones. Circuit items carry the claimed and the true value.

items.goal: Riders 120 cm and taller may ride.
items.why: height > 120 turns away a rider who is exactly 120 cm. "120 and taller" needs >=.
items.check: assert can_ride(120) and can_ride(150) and not can_ride(119)

items.goal: Under 12 is child, 12 to 64 is adult, 65 and over is senior.
items.why: elif only runs when age < 12 was False, so that branch really means 12 to 64. Every boundary lands in the right place.
items.check: assert ticket(11) == 'child' and ticket(12) == 'adult' and ticket(64) == 'adult' and ticket(65) == 'senior'

items.goal: True on Saturday and Sunday only.
items.why: "Sun" on its own is a non-empty string, which is always truthy, so every day counts as the weekend. Write day == "Sat" or day == "Sun".
items.check: assert is_weekend('Sat') and is_weekend('Sun') and not is_weekend('Mon')

items.goal: Add the numbers up to (not including) the first negative one.
items.why: continue skips the negative but keeps looping, so numbers after it are still added. Stopping at the first negative needs break.

items.goal: Count how many halvings take n down to 1.
items.why: n shrinks on every pass, so the test n > 1 is bound to turn False. 8, 4, 2, 1 is three steps.
items.check: assert halvings(8) == 3 and halvings(1) == 0 and halvings(9) == 3

items.goal: The index of the first even number, or len(nums) if there is none.
items.why: The guard runs too late: nums[i] is read before i < len(nums) is checked, so a list with no even number crashes. Put the length check first.

items.goal: The last three items of a list.
items.why: A slice stops before its end index, so -1 drops the very last item. items[-3:] keeps all three.

items.goal: Every even number from 0 up to and including n.
items.why: range stops before its end, so the + 1 lets n itself in when it is even.

items.goal: The middle item of a list with an odd length.
items.why: For 3 items, len // 2 is already 1, the middle index. Adding 1 points one past it.

items.goal: area(3, 4) gives 12.
items.why: Without a return statement a function hands back None, so area(3, 4) is None. Add return result.

items.goal: True if any number in the list is negative.
items.why: return False sits inside the loop, so the function gives up after checking only the first number. It belongs after the loop.

items.goal: A sorted copy, leaving the original list alone.
items.why: sorted() builds and returns a new list. (nums.sort() would sort in place and return None.)

items.goal: Each call adds one to the global count and returns it.
items.why: Assigning to count inside tick makes count local, so count += 1 reads a local with no value yet: UnboundLocalError. Add global count.

items.goal: Each call to step() counts up by one: 1, 2, 3 ...
items.why: nonlocal n lets step update the n that belongs to make_counter, so the count survives between calls.

items.goal: With no list given, return a new list holding just the tag.
items.why: The default list is made once, when def runs, and every call shares it, so tags pile up. Use tags=None and make a new list inside.

items.goal: age_text comes from input(), like "14". Return next year's age, 15.
items.why: Text from input() is a str, and str + int raises TypeError. Convert first: int(age_text) + 1.

items.goal: The mean of a list, or 0 for an empty list.
items.why: The empty-list guard comes before the division, so len(nums) is never 0 when it divides.

items.goal: label("Ana", 9) gives "Ana scored 9".
items.why: score is an int, and joining it to strings with + raises TypeError. Use str(score) or an f-string.

items.goal: A 9 V battery drives a 3 kΩ resistor. Find the current.
items.why: 3 kΩ is 3000 Ω. I = 9 / 3000 = 0.003 A, which is 3 mA, not 3 A.

items.goal: 20 mA flows through a 250 Ω resistor. Find the voltage.
items.why: Convert mA to A first, then V = I × R = 0.02 × 250 = 5 V.

items.goal: 12 V across a resistor drives 4 mA. Find its resistance.
items.why: 4 mA is 0.004 A, so R = 12 / 0.004 = 3000 Ω, which is 3 kΩ.

items.goal: 1 kΩ and 2 kΩ in series on 9 V. Find the current, in mA.
items.why: Series resistances add to 3 kΩ, and the same 3 mA flows through both parts.

items.goal: 12 V across 1 kΩ and 3 kΩ in series. Voltage across the 3 kΩ?
items.why: Voltage divides in proportion to resistance, not evenly: 3 mA × 3 kΩ = 9 V across the bigger resistor.

items.goal: Two resistors in series; 4 mA flows through the first. Current in the second, in mA?
lines: The current splits between the two
items.why: A series loop has only one path, so the same 4 mA flows through every part.

items.goal: 9 V across 1 kΩ and 3 kΩ in parallel. Voltage across each branch?
items.why: Each parallel branch is connected straight across the battery, so each one sees the full 9 V.

items.goal: 6 V across parallel 2 kΩ and 3 kΩ. Total current, in mA?
items.why: Each branch has the full 6 V across it, and branch currents add: 5 mA.

items.goal: Two 2 kΩ resistors in parallel. Combined resistance, in kΩ?
items.why: Adding is for series. Two equal parallel branches give current two paths, halving the resistance to 1 kΩ.

items.goal: A 9 V series loop where R2 is open. Current, in mA?
lines: The loop is broken at R2
items.why: A break leaves no complete path, so no current flows anywhere in the loop.

items.goal: A 9 V series loop where R2 is open. Meter across R2?
items.why: With no current, the good parts drop 0 V, so the full 9 V shows up across the gap at R2.

items.goal: A 9 V series loop where R2 is open. Meter across the good R1?
lines: R1 is still in the loop
items.why: No current flows, so V = I × R = 0 across R1. The full 9 V sits across the open part instead.

items.goal: Three equal resistors in series on 12 V; the middle one is shorted. Meter across it?
lines: A short is a wire across the part
items.why: A wire has no resistance, so nothing drops across the shorted part: 0 V.

items.goal: Three equal resistors in series on 12 V; the middle one is shorted. Meter across each good one?
lines: The good ones still read 4 V
items.why: The 12 V now splits over two resistors instead of three, so each good one reads 6 V.

items.goal: Two 1 kΩ resistors in series on 10 V; one is shorted. Current, in mA?
items.why: Only 1 kΩ is left in the loop, so the current doubles: 10 / 1000 = 10 mA.

items.goal: A resistor reads 6 V with 2 mA through it. Its real value, in kΩ?
items.why: Convert 2 mA to 0.002 A, then R = V / I = 3000 Ω.

items.goal: Labelled 1 kΩ: 5 V across it with 2.5 mA flowing. Its real value, in kΩ?
items.why: 5 / 0.0025 = 2000 Ω = 2 kΩ, double the label, so it is the wrong part.

items.goal: Labelled 470 Ω: it reads 4.7 V at 1 mA. Its real value, in Ω?
items.why: 4.7 / 0.001 = 4700 Ω, ten times the label: a 4.7 kΩ part fitted by mistake.
